Article Title: EPFO, officers' body contest claims about new IT system
Article Text:
EPFO has dismissed these and said this transition was implemented with minimal disruption of services, and the temporary increase in pendency was due to moving to a new enterprise-wide platform

NEW DELHI: Weeks after the rollout of the new centralised IT enabled system (CITES) early July by Employees' Provident Fund Organisation ( EPFO ), which promised to enhance member convenience through faster automated claims settlements, field officials across the country have been "left to their own devices" to deal with the mounting claim pendencies as the new system faces strain, claimed the EPF Officers Association (EPFOA) in a letter to labour minister Mansukh Mandaviya.Contrary to expectations that the majority of claims would be settled in 2-3 days, EPFOA claims that "lakhs of auto claims were kept pending in the system for more than 20 days, with no explanation to either the field offices or to the members."However, EPFO has dismissed these and said this transition was implemented with minimal disruption of services, and the temporary increase in pendency was due to moving to a new enterprise-wide platform.

EPF Officers Association (EPFOA) claims that "lakhs of auto claims were kept pending in the system for more than 20 days, with no explanation to either the field offices or to the members"

Article Title: Captain moves crew to citadel, thwarts pirate assault on India-bound vessel
Article Text:
After bringing all crew members into the ‘citadel’, the master of the Golden Arsenal sought help from the Indian Navy, which responded swiftly to the distress call (Representative image)

NEW DELHI: On July 1, an attack by pirates on an India-bound bulk carrier, Golden Arsenal, in the Gulf of Aden was foiled after the captain moved all crew members, including an Indian seafarer, into the vessel’s “citadel” and sought assistance from the Indian Navy A citadel is a fortified safe room with essential supplies such as food and water, as well as communication equipment, where crew members can take refuge during a pirate attack. The pirates failed to breach the citadel and eventually fled the vessel.Sharing this incident at the National Port Security Conference this week, Captain Vikram Singh Manhas, deputy nautical adviser at DGMA (maritime regulator), urged all crew members and masters to remain vigilant and follow preventive measures prescribed under best management practices (BMP), amid a rise in piracy incidents.Four vessels are held hostage by Somali pirates at present, three of which have Indian crew members aboard.One of the vessels has one Indian seafarer, while the other two have five and 11 Indian crew, respectively.Highlighting the significance of prevention in such cases, Manhas said that once a vessel is held by pirates, everything is dependent upon the negotiations with the pirates and that the government is working to ensure the safe release of Indian seafarers.In the direction of ensuring their safety, the government is set to launch a dashboard on August 15 to track every Indian seafarer on any ship. Additionally, shipping and ports minister Sarbananda Sonowal Saturday launched e-Samudra, a digital platform integrating services for seafarers, shipping companies, ports and other maritime stakeholders, and said, “Every Indian seafarer must be safe, respected and supported as India strengthens its position as a global maritime power. ”
Article Summary: On July 1, an attack by pirates on an India-bound bulk carrier, Golden Arsenal, in the Gulf of Aden was foiled. The captain moved all crew members, including an Indian seafarer, into the vessel’s ‘citadel’ and sought assistance from the Indian Navy. A citadel is a fortified safe room with essential supplies such as food and water, as well as communication equipment.

NEW DELHI: The law ministry notified the appointments of 30 judges for the high courts of Madras, Calcutta, Karnataka and MP on Saturday. The highest number of 15 judges have been appointed in the Madras high court , followed by eight in the Calcutta high court, six in Karnataka high court and one in MP high court.There are 25 high courts in the country; together they had 341 vacancies against a sanctioned strength of 1,112 judges.In the latest notifications, of the 30 appointments, seven are judicial officers who have been elevated to the HC benches, while 23 are advocates. Some of them have been appointed permanent judges, while most others have been appointed as additional judges for a two-year tenure, after which they will be evaluated and considered for being made a permanent judge.In the 25 high courts across the country, over 60 lakh cases are pending, of which 80,000 cases are pending for over three decades.The law minister has blamed the respective HC collegium for not following the timeline prescribed for initiating recommendations for appointments of judges for the HCs, the primary reason behind large vacancies. The HC collegium comprises the chief justice and two senior-most judges of the HC.

Article Title: Captain of turbulence-hit Phuket-Delhi flight may have failed dope test
Article Text:
The Airbus A320 with 145 people on board had encountered severe turbulence near Odisha and then suddenly dropped 300 feet.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: The captain operating Air India’s turbulence-hit Phuket-Delhi flight on Tuesday (Aug 4) reportedly tested positive in a psychoactive substances (dope) test conducted on arrival, according to multiple sources. The airline did not either confirm or deny it, saying while the tests were conducted, the results have not been shared with it.“We are aware that a post-flight screening test was conducted on the pilots in accordance with applicable protocols. However, the results of the test have not been shared with Air India, and we are therefore not in a position to comment on any findings,” an AI spokesperson said.“Air India undertakes regular drug testing of crew members in compliance with civil aviation regulations, independent of any specific flight or operational incident. We will continue to cooperate with the relevant authorities as required,” the airline added.The Airbus A320 with 145 people on board had encountered severe turbulence near Odisha and then suddenly dropped 300 feet. On arrival in Delhi, 13 passengers and four crew members were hospitalised. Sources say the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) is probing this case from all angles including whether the handling of this turbulence event was correct; whether the event happened due to weather or some other reason; the likely impact on the aircraft like did it suffer hydraulic failure due to impact and whether it should have flown all the way to Delhi after the episode and not diverted to some nearby airport like Varanasi or Lucknow.Pending probe, flight crew is taken off flying duty as per protocol. So the pilots of this flight are also not flying currently. DGCA rules stipulate that a pilot testing positive for consumption of psychoactive substances for the first time be referred to for de-addiction and rehabilitation. Such crew member can return for active duties with a negative dope test report.But after resuming flying if the same person tests positive for psychoactive substances again, their licence will be suspended for three years. And if after resuming flying the same person again tests positive for the third time, the flying licence is cancelled.International Civil Aviation Organisation says that “holders of licences shall not exercise the privileges of their licences and related ratings while under the influence of any psychoactive substance, which might render them unable to safely and properly exercise these privileges”.While the probe in Tuesday’s event would have focused on pilot handling the situation anyway, the captain reportedly testing positive adds another dimension to the same.
Article Summary: The Airbus A320 with 145 people on board had encountered severe turbulence near Odisha and then suddenly dropped 300 feet. On arrival in Delhi, 13 passengers and four crew members were hospitalised. The Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) is probing this case from all angles.

NEW DELHI: Sonam Wangchuk said his wife Gitanjali had tried to get Rahul Gandhi to offer him juice to end his 26-day hunger strike at Jantar Mantar but received no positive response, leaving him disappointed with the Congress leader and other political parties."We were pondering on breaking my fast through Rahul Gandhi ji and Gitanjali was working on that," Wangchuk told India Today. Wangchuk said she had made several strong comments against BJP and Hindutva forces as well, but while they kept quiet, the Congress "ecosystem" turned on her for criticising Gandhi."There were four or five very harsh comments about BJP. They didn't react, but the (Congress) ecosystem started trolling her, trolling me," he said. "I am disappointed with the leadership. He said he had studied the organisation and found its members "very well-meaning, fair and just and for the right cause, not aligned to any party as such".He welcomed CJP's decision to remain an apolitical pressure group instead of contesting polls. Article Title: Tarun Tejpal sentenced to 10 years' rigorous imprisonment in 2013 rape case; gets two weeks to surrender
Article Text:
Bombay HC convicts Tarun Tejpal in 2013 rape case, sentences him to 10 years' rigorous imprisonment

PANAJI: Thirteen years after the arrest of a high profile editor-in-chief of Tehelka magazine, Tarun Tejpal , for rape in an elevator of a starred hotel, the Bombay high court on Thursday found him guilty of rape and sentenced him to ten years Rigorous imprisonment.The HC has granted him two weeks time to surrender.The sentence was pronounced in the State's challenge to Tejpal's acquittal by the trial court in 2021.After the court found him guilty, senior advocate Aabad Ponda representing Tejpal sought lenient sentence for him on the grounds that he is a senior citizen today, aged 62 and that the case is a 13 year old one.Tejpal addressing the division bench of Justices Dr Neela Gokhale and Amit Jamsandekar said he is a "political victim" and is 62 years old and a father of two with a wife and sought a lenient sentence.He said that there is so much evidence in favour of him that he can be acquitted ten times.Solicitor general of India representing Goa Government Tushar Mehta however argued for maximum sentence for Tejpal. He urged the court to consider that Tejpal was old enough to be in a parental position vis-a vis the survivor and argued that the sentence should set a precedent and have a strong deterrent effect.Mehta said that this was not some "misunderstanding or some banter" and pointed out that Tejpal had no remorse after the incident and alleged that he repeated the same thing on the next day.He said Tejpal was brazen despite resistance and despite the survivor saying no.He further argued that the survivor's mature conduct after the incident had been wrongly portrayed as that of someone who had enjoyed the molestation."It is high time the highest constitutional court of the state gives him the maximum sentence. No means No. You may be whosoever you are but when a girl says no it means no. That deterrent message may be considered," Mehta told the court while arguing on maximum sentence for him.Mehta during the hearings seeking Tejpal's conviction argued that the survivor was a stellar witness and stood by her case and that Tejpal's apology to her was proof of what he had done. He also argued that there was no reason for a man of her father's age to send her such her the 'the fingertips' text message after midnight and that it could not reasonably have an innocent meaning. Ponda had countered that saying the 'fingertips' text message had a different context and did not prove charge of rape.He had argued that the survivor had a "propensity to lie" and that her behaviour after the alleged incident was not commensurate with someone who had been raped and traumatised.
Article Summary: Bombay HC convicts Tarun Tejpal in 2013 rape case, sentences him to 10 years' rigorous imprisonment. The HC has granted him two weeks time to surrender. After the court found him guilty, senior advocate Aabad Ponda sought lenient sentence for him.

Article Title: Explainer: What changes as Parliament passes Registration of Births and Deaths Bill
Article Text:
The Parliament passed the Registration of Births and Deaths (Amendment) Bill, 2026.

What does the Bill change?

What is the significance of a birth certificate?

What happened in the Parliament?

There are govts in some states that look for an opportunity and welcome those (who were not born in India) and register their births who are not eligible to be registered here. Now, we will not allow this to happen. Union minister of state for home Nityanand Rai

What is the significance of the bill

Why did the opposition say

The Parliament passed the Registration of Births and Deaths (Amendment) Bill, 2026, amid a wider logjam that has repeatedly disrupted the Monsoon Session. The Rajya Sabha cleared the legislation on Tuesday by voice vote days after the Lok Sabha passed it on July 31 amid opposition protests without a debate.Both Houses witnessed repeated adjournments during the session, with several Bills being passed amid disruptions. The Monsoon Session began on July 20 and is scheduled to conclude on August 13.The new legislation focuses on a seemingly routine but important part of government records like registering births and deaths. A birth certificate records a person's entry into the official system, while a death certificate formally records their departure.Together, these documents help establish identity, maintain public records and provide proof for a range of legal and administrative purposes. The amendment seeks to tighten the process when such events are reported long after they occur.Under the existing system, delayed registration already requires additional verification. If information about a birth or death is submitted after one year but within two years, the amended law will require an order from a district magistrate, sub-divisional magistrate or an executive magistrate authorised by the district magistrate.For cases reported more than two years after the event, the threshold becomes higher. The registration will require an order from a judicial magistrate of the First Class having jurisdiction over the place where the birth or death occurred.The magistrate will have to verify the correctness of the information before permitting registration. A prescribed fee will also have to be paid, according to a document released by the government.The amendment also updates the reference to an "Executive Magistrate" in the 1969 law to align it with the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, which replaced the earlier Code of Criminal Procedure.The government says the primary objective is to ensure that births and deaths are registered promptly and that delayed registrations are subjected to stronger scrutiny.The Registration of Births and Deaths Act makes registration mandatory. According to the government's statement of objects and reasons, birth and death certificates provide legal identity and can be used as evidence of a person's birth or death.The government argues that the integrity of these records is particularly important because birth certificates can be used for several official purposes, including processes involving identity and citizenship-related documentation.Tighter scrutiny of delayed registrations, it says, can help prevent fraudulent or questionable entries and improve the reliability of official records.BJP IT cell head Amit Malviya said, “The objective is straightforward: encourage timely registration, prevent fraudulent or dubious entries, and preserve the credibility of birth and death certificates, the foundational documents that establish a person’s legal identity.”The government has also pointed to a significant rise in registration rates over the past decade.Union minister of state for home Nityanand Rai said birth registration increased from 86.6% in 2014 to 99.1% in 2024, while death registration rose from 72.5% to 99.4% during the same period. He also said around 3.5 lakh registration centres have been established across the country.The government's argument is that as registration coverage approaches universal levels, the focus must increasingly be on ensuring that the remaining delayed or questionable cases are properly verified.A birth certificate is often the first formal document linking an individual to the state. It records details such as a person's date and place of birth and can be required for a range of official purposes, including education, employment, passports and other government documentation.The government has also highlighted the role of birth records in establishing identity and in processes where proof of birth or citizenship-related documentation is required.That makes the accuracy of the registration system important beyond population statistics.A fraudulent birth certificate, for instance, could potentially affect records across several government systems. Similarly, failure to register deaths can leave outdated information in official databases.The government has also linked accurate death registration with keeping records, including electoral rolls, updated.The Lok Sabha passed the Bill on July 31 by voice vote amid opposition protests. Several opposition MPs entered the Well of the House demanding the presence of Union home minister Amit Shah , and the legislation was cleared without a debate.Parliamentary affairs minister Kiren Rijiju criticised the opposition for not participating in the proceedings and said the government wanted a discussion on the "important Bill".“It is unfortunate. Please do not repeat this in the future. People who sent you to Parliament will seek answers from you,” Rijiju said, urging MPs to participate in debates rather than disrupt proceedings.The legislation was passed amid continued sloganeering, with the opposition MPs demanding the presence of Union home minister Amit Shah and his response on the "police action" against student protesters on July 20 at Jantar Mantar.The Rajya Sabha later took up the Bill amid similar disruptions.Moving the Bill in the Rajya Sabha, Rai said the government wanted every birth and death to be properly recorded. He said, “The country wants that anyone born in the country, it is important that he or she is registered. Anyone who has died, cannot continue to remain in the voter lists to benefit some parties.”Rai also linked the legislation to concerns over people who have died continuing to appear on electoral rolls.He also cited the rise in registration rates as evidence of the government's efforts to improve the system.Some NDA members supported the legislation. YSRCP member M R Reddy, AIADMK's M Thambidurai and BRS member Ravi Chandra Vaddiraju backed the Bill. BJP member Biswajit Sinha, meanwhile, accused the Congress of opposing the legislation because it did not want proper registration of births and deaths.Sinha also referred to the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls in West Bengal, claiming that people who had died years earlier remained on voter lists.He alleged that some parties were helping illegal Bangladeshi and Pakistani infiltrators obtain birth registrations and voter identities, and said the proposed changes would help prevent such practices.Leader of opposition Mallikarjun Kharge said, “The prime minister and the home minister should come. we want discussion.”Despite the protests, the Bill was taken up for consideration and passage.Opposition members did not reject the need for accurate birth and death records but questioned the practical implications of requiring a Judicial Magistrate of the First Class to approve registrations delayed by more than two years.UPPL member Pramod Boro said the objective of the Bill was important but questioned whether an administrative responsibility should be shifted to the judiciary.He warned that the provision could add to the workload of courts, increase costs and make registration more difficult for migrants, homeless people, poor families and those living in remote areas.BJD member Santrupt Misra also questioned why registrations are delayed in the first place. He suggested that the government should identify the reasons behind late registration and consider dedicated registration offices, particularly in tribal areas, to improve access.CPI(M) member V Sivadasan supported the need for proper registration but said the government should also focus on the circumstances surrounding deaths, including malnutrition and student deaths.The passage came amid a wider logjam in the Monsoon Session, with repeated adjournments in both Houses and several Bills being cleared amid disruptions.With Parliament having passed the Bill, the legislation will now go through the remaining constitutional process before coming into force. The Bill, therefore, seeks to strike a balance between two objectives: ensuring that births and deaths are recorded promptly, while subjecting unusually delayed registrations to greater scrutiny.
Article Summary: The Parliament passed the Registration of Births and Deaths (Amendment) Bill, 2026. The Rajya Sabha cleared the legislation on Tuesday by voice vote. The Lok Sabha passed it on July 31 amid opposition protests without a debate. Both Houses witnessed repeated adjournments during the session, with several Bills being passed amid disruptions.

Article Title: Proposed MDR for UPI transactions will be nominal, says government
Article Text:
Government officials have indicated that MDR of 0.25% to 0.4% may be allowed for UPI transactions above Rs 2,000, with a ceiling on the charge.

NEW DELHI: The government said on Saturday that the proposed merchant discount rate (MDR) for UPI transactions will be nominal and apply only to a limited set of merchants for transactions above a threshold, while seeking to assure users that all person-to-person transactions will remain free and consumers who make the payment will not face any fees."A vast majority of the transactions will remain free of charge for merchants on UPI. MDR, if introduced, will only be threshold-based and not levied on a blanket basis to all," the statement said, adding that the UPI and Services Steering Committee, headed by NPCI, will decide on the MDR, if any.It also dismissed reports of the charges being imposed under pressure from the US, which was seen to be pushing the case of Visa and Mastercard that levy MDR on credit card and debit card transactions, which are up to 2%, and usually not passed on to consumers unless the merchant is keen on a cash transaction. "If external pressure had been a factor, the government would not have introduced UPI in 2016 or made it free of charge for both merchants as well as citizens since Jan 2020 and ensured that it became the world's largest real-time interoperable payment system.The amendment should be viewed in the context of the government's broader objective of ensuring that India's digital payment infrastructure remains sustainable, competitive, and capable of serving the country's rapidly expanding digital economy."The finance ministry argued the move was necessary to expand the infrastructure into rural and semi-urban areas. Officials have indicated an MDR of 0.25% to 0.4% may be allowed for UPI transactions above Rs 2,000, provided they are not person-to-person, with a ceiling on the charge.
Article Summary: The proposed merchant discount rate (MDR) for UPI transactions will be nominal and apply only to a limited set of merchants for transactions above a threshold. A vast majority of the transactions will remain free of charge for merchants on UPI. The finance ministry argued the move was necessary to expand the infrastructure into rural and semi-urban areas.

Article Title: Government spending on education below Unesco's 15% standard
Article Text:
The scorecard concludes that, on average, countries are "moving away" from the public education expenditure benchmarks of at least 4% of GDP or 15% of total public expenditure.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: India remains just above Unesco's minimum GDP benchmark for education, but the sector's share in government spending has slipped below the prescribed threshold. Education accounts for 4.1% of GDP but 14.2% of total public expenditure, down from 15.7% in 2015 and below the 15% benchmark, Unesco's 2026 SDG 4 scorecard has shown.The funding picture assumes significance because India continues to lag on secondary school completion. Its latest lower secondary (Classes VI-VIII) completion rate is 86% as against its 99% national benchmark for 2025, while upper secondary (Classes IX-XII) completion rate is 51% as against 84%. Unesco classifies progress at both levels as slow.Under the Education 2030 framework, countries committed to spending 4-6% of GDP and/or 15-20% of public expenditure on education. The scorecard uses the lower thresholds as minimum benchmarks. India meets one. Its spending on education has remained at 4.1% of GDP since 2015, but its share of public expenditure has declined 1.5 percentage points to 14.2%.Among major emerging economies, China too meets one benchmark, at 4% of GDP (11.9% of public spending), while figures for Brazil are 5.6% and 12.9%. South Africa meets both, at 6% and 19.1%, while Indonesia, Bangladesh and Pakistan meet neither.The pattern is common among developed economies too: the US, UK, Germany and France meet the GDP threshold but not the public expenditure benchmark, while Sweden and Switzerland meet both.Unesco noted that richer countries tend to meet the GDP benchmark but not the public expenditure threshold because they raise more revenue, while education often accounts for a larger share of budgets in poorer countries.Latest data show 39 of 205 countries, or 19%, meeting both benchmarks, while 72, or 35%, meet neither. Another 64 countries, including India, spend above 4% of GDP but below 15% of public expenditure. Among high-income countries, 11% meet both benchmarks and 50% follow India's pattern.India, however, has larger unmet schooling needs. Lower secondary completion has risen from 81% in 2015 to 86% but remains 13 percentage points below its 99% benchmark. Even Unesco's "feasible" 2025 benchmark of 90% is four points above the latest rate.This is despite programmes operating at scale. Unesco's India profile says Samagra Shiksha supports about 15.6 crore learners, while PM-Poshan covers around 11.8 crore children in 11.2 lakh government and aided schools. The trend is part of a broader global concern. The scorecard concludes that, on average, countries are "moving away" from the public education expenditure benchmarks of at least 4% of GDP or 15% of total public expenditure.
Article Summary: Education accounts for 4.1% of GDP but 14.2% of total public expenditure. This is down from 15.7% in 2015 and below the 15% benchmark, Unesco says. The funding picture assumes significance because India continues to lag on secondary school completion.

Article Title: Kashmir route outpaces Manali as Ladakh tourism surges
Article Text:
The spokesman said the surge in tourist arrivals during June and July has also been supported by a calendar of cultural, spiritual and experiential events organised across Ladakh

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

SRINAGAR: Ladakh continues to witness a surge in tourist arrivals, with the union territory recording 330,332 tourists from Jan to July this year, already reaching 98.35% of the 335,872 tourists recorded last year, a govt spokesman said.Air travel remained the most popular mode of reaching Ladakh, accounting for 47.64% of the total arrivals. Among tourists arriving by road, the Kashmir route continued to be more popular than the Manali route, with 35.27% entering Ladakh through Kashmir compared with 17.09% through Manali, according to the latest figures released by the Ladakh govt.“The surge in tourism numbers has been particularly noticeable in June and July, when more than 2.12 lakh tourists visited Ladakh, accounting for nearly 65% of the total 3.30 lakh tourist arrivals recorded so far this year,” the spokesman said.He said the growth in tourism coincides with a major and rapid transformation in Ladakh’s connectivity infrastructure since the formation of the UT. “The total road network has increased from 1,799 km in 2019 to over 4,200 km in 2026, while the number of bridges has increased from 19 to 72,” he added.He said the period of seasonal disruption on key routes has also reduced substantially. Zoji La, the gateway to Ladakh from Kashmir, which earlier remained closed for around 127 days annually, now remains closed for only 16 days.“Similarly, the annual closure of the Kargil-Zanskar Road has declined from 154 days to 11 days, significantly improving near-year-round connectivity for tourists,” he said, adding that the number of homestays has increased from 128 in 2019 to 2,275 in 2026, creating new livelihood opportunities for local households.The spokesman said the surge in tourist arrivals during June and July has also been supported by a calendar of cultural, spiritual and experiential events organised across Ladakh.Lieutenant Governor Vinai Kumar Saxena, in a statement, attributed the growing tourist footfall, particularly domestic tourism, to the sustained infrastructure development in Ladakh and the appeal of PM Narendra Modi to citizens to visit tourist places in India and promote domestic tourism.“The fact that Ladakh has crossed the 1 lakh mark in tourist arrivals for two successive months and has already achieved more than 98% of the entire 2025 footfall by the end of July is a very encouraging milestone,” Saxena said.
Article Summary: Ladakh continues to witness a surge in tourist arrivals, with the union territory recording 330,332 tourists from Jan to July this year. Air travel remained the most popular mode of reaching Ladakh, accounting for 47.64% of the total arrivals. Among tourists arriving by road, the Kashmir route continued to be more popular than the Manali route.

NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday participated in the 57th convocation ceremony of the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Delhi, where he presented the institute’s highest honours to meritorious students.At the event, PM Modi urged IIT Delhi graduates to encourage greater participation and representation of women in academic and professional achievements, noting that only a few female students had received medals at the ceremony.PM Modi congratulated the award-winning students but said there should have been "more" girls among them."Many students have received medals for their achievements. I extend my heartiest congratulations to all of you. However, it would have been even better if there were a few more girls among them. Sorry. Why just one or two? Article Title: JPSC, E20, anti-reservation: The issues India is talking about
Article Text:
CJP’s success may have opened the door for the next big youth movement, but what issue can turn online anger into real-world action?

Eyes on Jharkhand

E20

Containers displayed as purported fuel samples are seen during an Indian Youth Congress (IYC) protest against E20 fuel policy (PTI)

Lack of jobs

Anti-reservation movement

RHA’s Insta page has gained significant followers

CJP's spokesperson Ashutosh Ranka brings focus on lack of jobs

RHA has posted five broad demands:

Political parties be barred from promising new or higher reservation quotas during elections.

The 50% limit on caste-based reservation should not be breached.

Set a time-bound roadmap to improve government schools, teachers and educational infrastructure.

As educational inequality reduces, reservation should be gradually phased out.

Reservation should be reviewed every 10 years using updated socio-economic data.

Reservation lists should be updated periodically, moving communities that have progressed to the General category.

Members of Swarn Samaj and Brahman Parivar stage a protest against the UGC's new caste-based equity rules at Hazratganj, in Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh in January (PTI)

Pollution

Anti-pollution protest: Protesters last year showing posters of Maoist commander Madvi Hidma, who was killed in an encounter (PTI)

So, what actually makes people protest?

Why CJP clicked with India’s youth: Anger, accessibility and a platform to be heard

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

India just witnessed the 'reel' generation make the 'real' world listen. July 2026 saw something Indian parents have dreamt of for years: Gen Z looked up from its screens. But it was for a cause. They turned memes into megaphones and forced the country to pay attention to exam reforms. In their own language, they ate and left no crumbs.Exam paper leaks weren't new. Student protests weren't either. What was different was how a "cockroach" remark snowballed into a meme, then into the Cockroach Janata Party, and eventually into a nationwide movement that dominated headlines.Now comes the bigger question: What other issues is India talking about?While the CJP protest has ended, the demand for a system overhaul has not. As Jantar Mantar went quiet, Jharkhand emerged as the new battleground as students demand accountability over JPSC-JSSC exam irregularities.Student leader Devendra Nath Mahto has been on a hunger strike since August 2, while protesters are seeking an independent probe and reforms in the recruitment process.Then there is E20, a policy that directly affects vehicle owners.The nationwide rollout of 20% ethanol-blended petrol has sparked a political and online debate over mileage, older vehicle compatibility and whether the Centre followed the phased roadmap laid out by NITI Aayog.After the NEET protests, calls for Union minister Nitin Gadkari's resignation began circulating, while leaders including Arvind Kejriwal and Rahul Gandhi also raised the issue.Vivek Rajput, a CA at a top government firm, says that although he has never attended a protest, this might become his first. “If there is a protest over E20, I will definitely go. My vehicle’s mileage has gone down compared to before.”CJP spokesperson Ashutosh Ranka agrees that E20 deserves attention, but questions whether the government has adequately addressed concerns around its impact and benefits. “Obviously, E20 is an important issue that needs to be addressed. I don't think the government has very scientifically backed data to suggest whether the vehicles would be impacted or not,” Ranka said.“Neither has there been any clarification on why the prices haven't dropped as it was promised to us. So what exactly has ethanol E20 petrol achieved in the country? There is no sort of clarity on that.”India’s job crisis is particularly acute among its growing pool of educated young people. According to the State of Working India 2026 report, the number of young graduates rose nearly 13-fold from about 5 million in 1983 to 63 million in 2023, but graduate unemployment among those below 25 remains close to 40%. The number of unemployed graduates has also surged 16-fold, from less than 1 million to around 11 million over the same period. Government data points to continued pressure: youth unemployment among 15-29-year-olds reached 16.2% in June 2026, even as their labour force participation rate fell to 40.3%. The figures highlight a widening gap between the number of young people entering the workforce and the availability of secure, quality jobs.Anger has also been growing over the increasing tax burden on common people. “As the finance minister, Nirmala Sitharaman is not giving enough tax benefits to salaried people. Under the old tax regime, at least people could save money and also save on taxes. Now, neither are we able to save, nor are we getting tax benefits," said Rajput.Reservation Hatao Andolan (RHA) recently gained nearly 6 million followers on Instagram. “Backed by citizens who feel left behind by reservation politics and driven by merit. The brave earn respect through their character and perseverance. Only the cowardly and the cruel keep shouting about caste,” the Insta bio of the page reads.The page was formed in October last year and the first post was made in March this year. Since the CJP protest, the account became more active.But quota has been a divisive issue in India. Unlike the paper-leak issue, which is an offence and affects students across categories, reservation is a constitutional policy rooted in questions of representation, historical disadvantage and unequal access — and does not attract a unified opinion.The merit debate also gets complicated when cut-offs enter the picture. In 2023, when the NEET-PG qualifying percentile was reduced to zero for all categories amid thousands of vacant seats, candidates who had fallen below the original cut-off became eligible for admission. General-category candidates accounted for the largest share of those admitted after the reduction — over 56%, compared with 26% OBC, 11% SC and 6% ST. The skew was sharper in private colleges, where General-category candidates accounted for around 70% of those who secured clinical specialities after the cut-off was lowered. The data does not suggest that General-category candidates were given a special concession; rather, it shows that they formed the largest share of those who benefited from the relaxation.Caste-based reservation in education has been part of India's affirmative-action framework for decades. Before independence, several rulers and institutions had experimented with measures to uplift historically disadvantaged communities. After independence, the Constitution formally provided for reservation for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, which was later expanded to other backward classes and, in a different form, economically weaker sections.Those advocating against the existing quota system argue that it compromises merit and should be replaced or reworked around economic disadvantage.Income-based reservation: Under this, they demand that the reservation should purely be based on the income.One family, one reservation, one time: Under this, it demands that once a family has benefited from reservation, the next generation should compete on merit.Minimum standards for everyone: Under this, it demands that every exam should have minimum qualifying marks within 10-20% of the higher quota cut-off. If reserved seats fall vacant, it wants them allotted to the General category.No reservation politics: Under this, it demands:The sunset clause: Under this, it demands that no policy should run forever.CJP spokesperson Ashutosh Ranka, however, believes the reservation debate itself risks taking attention away from a larger problem: the shortage of opportunities.“I think the reservation-hatao movement, I just don't get the idea,” Ranka said. “The focus every time the debate is brought on reservation, that really means that people, there is a distraction from the broader issue.”For Ranka, that broader issue is jobs and seats. “There are only 2% of the jobs which are government jobs in this country, 98% of the jobs in this country are private sector jobs,” he said. “Why are there not enough jobs in this country? Why are there not enough government seats, medical seats, engineering seats in this country?”“Reservation, the topic of reservation is always a distraction on the broader structural issues which no one is ready to address. We need more jobs, we need more seats in colleges. That's what people should be asking,” he said.Others, however, see reservation itself as the issue that needs to be challenged.The matter has gained even more attention after the UGC rules. The UGC equity regulations have also become a potential flashpoint, with the 2026 rules aimed at addressing discrimination in higher education.The Supreme Court stayed the regulations in January, citing ambiguities and the possibility of misuse, but the issue has resurfaced amid growing anti-reservation sentiment online and could emerge as another potential trigger for youth mobilisation.But whether online traction can become a street movement remains an open question.Rajput said his brother sent him the Reservation Hatao Andolan page on Instagram and he started following it only last week. He said there were 21 people on his team with eight or nine belonging to the General category while the others benefited from reservation.For Rajput, however, the online movement has not yet translated into a willingness to protest on the ground. That distinction could prove crucial. After all, CJP's success was not simply about getting people to watch, like or share.But there is a counter-argument to the idea that reservation could become the next universal youth cause. Many SC/ST communities and other socially disadvantaged groups still lack equal access to quality education, particularly in rural areas where caste-based discrimination and social inequalities continue.So, unlike the paper-leak issue, where the grievance could unite students across categories, an anti-reservation movement begins with a built-in fault line.It may have the followers. It may have the slogans. It may even have people ready to take the fight to the streets. But whether it can replicate CJP's cross-sectional appeal is another question altogether.Diwali is just a couple of months away. And, as predictable as the festival itself, the annual debate will return: to burn or not to burn crackers.But for Delhi-NCR, pollution is not just a seasonal social-media debate. When the air turns toxic, the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) kicks in, bringing curbs that can affect everything from construction and traffic to office timings and schools. A study by IITM-Pune and CAQM found that without GRAP, Delhi could see 60% more severe-AQI hours, while the measures could reduce PM2.5 levels by up to 42 µg/m³, depending on the stage.In Mumbai too, pollution has emerged as a growing urban challenge, with construction and road dust, vehicle emissions and industrial activity among the key contributors to poor air quality. Pollution spikes have become a recurring concern, with several parts of the city recording AQI levels above 200, raising concerns over prolonged exposure to harmful particulate matter such as PM2.5. The problem adds to the wider challenges of rapid urbanisation, infrastructure growth and increasing vehicular traffic in the city.So, could pollution become the next rallying point, or is an issue with no single villain simply too difficult to turn into a movement? “If there is a protest over pollution, I’ll go for that too. I think we can raise our voice over issues that directly affect us. I would even join a protest over taxes,” said Rajput.The logic is simple: if an issue hits your lungs, your wallet or your everyday life, it may be easier to turn outrage into action.For Ratna Singh, CJP’s legal head, the answer isn't simply the issue itself. It is how that issue is packaged, communicated and mobilised.She believes CJP gained momentum because it was a Gen Z protest around education — an issue that extends well beyond NEET aspirants to competitive-exam candidates, school and college students, graduates and young people looking for jobs.Education, she said, allowed both Gen Z and Gen Alpha — and even their parents — to relate to the movement. “A lot of people in the crowd, when they were coming, they were like, you know, my parents were not letting me be here. But now I'm here. So they're also supporting,” Singh said.And then comes the part that may matter most for the next protest. “Something can trend on Instagram, but on ground, how you are planning it, how you are strategising it, that's also important,” Singh said.She added that people may relate to an issue online but still not turn up physically. How organisers convey the importance of an issue — and how they plan to keep an agitation going — can determine whether it survives beyond a social-media trend.That is perhaps the biggest lesson from CJP.Going viral can get an issue noticed. Mobilising people can turn it into a movement.Singh believes unemployment could be the next major youth issue. CJP is planning a nationwide “Kya Bolti Public” campaign in September to hear from young people across states about the problems they face.She said the organisation wants unemployment and education to become a more central part of the public conversation and wants to understand youth concerns and push for reforms. “With the success of Cockroach Janata Party, this wave has started, where people will come forward, people will talk about issues, people will also talk about unemployment and youth-related, youth-centric issues,” Singh said.Reservation has the Instagram audience. Pollution has the lived experience. E20 has the everyday grievance. Unemployment has the scale. But whichever issue wins the race will need to clear one final hurdle. It has to make people look up from their screens — and then actually leave them.
Article Summary: India just witnessed the'reel' generation make the'real' world listen. CJP's spokesperson Ashutosh Ranka brings focus on lack of jobs. The nationwide rollout of 20% ethanol-blended petrol has sparked a political and online debate.

Article Title: ‘Gangstran Te Vaar’: Punjab Police acts against over 58,000 criminals in 200-day crackdown
Article Text:
Punjab Police’s ‘Gangstran Te Vaar’ Completes 200 Days of Sustained Crackdown

Crackdown targets entire organised crime ecosystem

Weapons, drugs and criminal infrastructure seized

Overseas gangsters brought back

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Tipline launched for public intelligence

Punjab Police’s flagship anti-gangster campaign ‘Gangstran Te Vaar’ has completed 200 days, with the force claiming a major crackdown on organised crime networks across the state.During the campaign, police conducted 1,09,087 raids, arrested 1,532 proclaimed offenders and initiated action against 58,212 criminals and their associates, according to official sources.Launched under the Bhagwant Mann government, the intelligence-driven campaign has focused not only on gangsters but also on their associates, financial networks, weapons supply, logistics and overseas handlers.Police said preventive action was taken against 28,201 people, while another 18,514 were verified and released. Overall, the campaign covered 1,04,927 persons, including gangsters, their associates and wanted criminals.DGP Gaurav Yadav said the operation had evolved into a multi-dimensional campaign aimed at dismantling the ecosystem supporting organised crime.“Our strategy goes beyond arrests to dismantling the ecosystem that enables organised crime by targeting associates, finances, logistics, communication channels and overseas linkages,” Yadav said.The campaign also targeted the firepower and financial networks of organised gangs. Punjab Police recovered 990 illegal firearms, 242 sharp-edged weapons, 2,739 rounds of ammunition, 315 magazines, 2.5 kg of explosives and 15 hand grenades.In its action against the crime-drug nexus, police seized 774.38 kg of heroin, 480.23 kg of opium, 7,266.26 kg of poppy husk and more than 26.91 lakh intoxicant tablets.Authorities also seized Rs 1.73 crore in drug money, Rs 1.80 crore in cash and 413.85 grams of gold.The Anti-Gangster Task Force (AGTF) also pursued fugitives operating from abroad. Police highlighted the deportation of gangster Bhuvnesh Chopra alias Ashish Chopra from Central Asia and Jobanjit Singh alias Joban Billa from Jakarta, Indonesia.AGTF chief Pramod Ban said the campaign increasingly combines field operations with financial investigations, digital intelligence and coordination with central agencies to track foreign-based handlers and criminal networks.Punjab Police said 4,978 mobile handsets, 1,781 vehicles and 61 drones linked to criminal activities were also seized, while 64,402.77 litres of illicit liquor was recovered and destroyed.To strengthen public participation, the AGTF has launched a dedicated anonymous tipline at 93946-93946 for information about gangsters, wanted criminals and related activities. A reward policy has also been introduced for credible information leading to action against wanted criminals, with authorities promising confidentiality for informants.
Article Summary: Punjab Police’s flagship anti-gangster campaign ‘Gangstran Te Vaar’ has completed 200 days. Police conducted 1,09,087 raids, arrested 1,532 proclaimed offenders and initiated action against 58,212 criminals and their associates.

Article Title: 'Dard, data, daulat': Rahul Gandhi targets Centre over unemployment at ‘Chhatron Ki Goonj’ event
Article Text:
Rahul Gandhi addresses the gathering during the 'Chhatron Ki Goonj' program, in Prayagraj, Uttar Pradesh.

Poll Vote & Share your view Which factor do you think poses the biggest challenge to youth employment in India? Expensive education AI and technology Lack of available jobs 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

NEW DELHI: Congress leader Rahul Gandhi on Saturday described India’s youth as the country’s biggest strength, but said a lack of jobs, expensive education, paper leaks, poor access to credit and the growing use of AI were holding them back.Speaking at the ‘Chhatron Ki Goonj’ programme at KP Ground in Prayagraj, Rahul told the gathering, “You are power and pride of India; when I say this, I talk about every Indian citizen.” He said he wanted to speak about “dard (pain), data, and daulat (wealth)”, framing his address around the problems facing young Indians and the economic resources he believes should belong to them.Rahul said India’s nearly 40 crore young people were its “greatest strength”, adding that while there was much discussion about America, China and Russia, “India’s youth [are] unparalleled.” He argued that the country's future would depend on the potential of its young population and the data they generate.He said artificial intelligence was also built on people’s data and argued that this data should be treated as an asset belonging to Indians. Rahul criticised the growing use of AI in discussions about employment, saying technological changes could further threaten jobs unless young people benefited from the economy being built around their data.Rahul also spoke about his connection to Prayagraj, describing the city as his family’s home and recalling its past as an important educational centre. He said Allahabad University had once been among the country's best universities.Rahul said young Indians were being trapped in a “chakravyuh”, with education becoming increasingly expensive while degrees often failed to translate into jobs.“Today, education certificates have no meaning in India because they cannot give you job,” he said, arguing that students could spend years and large amounts of money on education without finding meaningful employment.Rahul said the problems extended across several routes into the workforce. “All doors of employment are closed in India,” he said, pointing to a decline in manufacturing, difficulties in securing loans, government-exam paper leaks and AI-driven job losses.“Decline in manufacturing, hard-to-come-by loans, paper leaks, AI replacing jobs – all this is hurting India's youth,” Rahul said.He blamed demonetisation and GST for hurting small industries, alleged that banks were failing to provide adequate credit to small and medium businesses, and criticised the privatisation of public-sector companies. He also argued that AI could further reduce corporate employment while young Indians were increasingly pushed towards gig work.Rahul framed these problems as part of what he called the broader “system”, arguing that economic and political power had become concentrated among a small number of people. He linked this to his criticism of large corporations, the government and the RSS, alleging that they exercised disproportionate influence over India's institutions.Rahul said recent student protests showed that young Indians were beginning to challenge the system. “Youths lit a light in darkness, and in doing so, changed the country,” he said.He urged young people to confront their fears without resorting to hatred or violence. “You cannot hate or be violent,” Rahul said, adding, “We will never resort to hatred or violence; will change the system with love and affection.”
Article Summary: Rahul Gandhi spoke at the 'Chhatron Ki Goonj' programme at KP Ground in Prayagraj. He said he wanted to speak about ‘dard (pain), data, and daulat (wealth)’ He argued that the country's future would depend on its young population.

Article Title: Bihar should withdraw alcohol ban as it failed to curb crimes against women: Report
Article Text:
Representative image

Ban failed to reduce crimes against women, says paper

Prohibition has also hit state revenues

Education, health and jobs among Bihar's priorities

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Bihar should withdraw its prohibition on alcohol as the ban has failed to reduce crimes against women and has been accompanied by a rise in illicit liquor and alternative intoxicants, according to a research paper by economic think tank National Council of Applied Economic Research (NCAER).The paper, titled ‘Macro Perspective of Bihar's Development Achievements, Unfinished Agenda, and the Way Forward’, also said restoring liquor excise duty to pre-ban levels could increase the state's own revenues by 14-15 per cent while reducing expenditure on enforcement and anti-smuggling operations.Prepared by a team of economists led by Ratna Sahay and presented at the India Policy Forum, the paper examined the economic and social impact of Bihar's prohibition, introduced in April 2016.The paper said the primary reasons for introducing prohibition were the belief that alcohol consumption contributed significantly to domestic violence and that households would redirect money previously spent on alcohol towards more productive uses.Women's groups and activists had also strongly backed the ban, arguing that prohibition would reduce alcohol-related abuse.However, the NCAER researchers said available data now allows an assessment of whether those objectives were achieved.“We now have sufficient data and information to assess if the ban was effective. Reported crimes against women in Bihar have not declined following the introduction of prohibition. Instead, total reported crimes against women increased over the post-2016 period,” the paper said.According to the study, the available evidence does not show a broad-based reduction in crimes against women after prohibition. Instead, it said the ban coincided with concerns over the expansion of illicit liquor networks, enforcement difficulties and corruption.The paper also pointed to increased use of alternative intoxicants, including illicit drugs.“In tandem, there was a significant rise in illegal liquor trade leading to higher alcohol consumption, increased crime and corruption, and an increase in the use of alternative additive substances, such as illicit drugs,” it said.The NCAER paper said Bihar suffered significant fiscal consequences after the ban. Before prohibition, excise duty on alcohol accounted for about 14 per cent of the state's own revenues in the three years preceding the ban.At the same time, the government incurred higher expenditure on monitoring, enforcement and anti-smuggling operations, which the paper said added to fiscal pressures.The researchers argued that reinstating liquor excise duty at historical levels could help restore the contribution of the tax to around 14 per cent of state revenues.The paper concluded that the prohibition had not achieved its intended objectives and had instead coincided with higher reported crimes against women, loss of state revenue and increased enforcement expenditure.Beyond prohibition, the paper identified six interconnected areas that it said should form the core of Bihar's development strategy: education, health, governance and law and order, flood mitigation, private-sector development and women's empowerment.It said reforms in these areas were necessary to improve productivity, accelerate structural transformation and create better-quality jobs for Bihar's young population.The study also examined the state's public debt and fiscal sustainability, and assessed the financing required for different reform scenarios. It called for a combination of stronger own-revenue mobilisation, more efficient public spending, additional central government support and, where necessary, further borrowing.The paper noted that improvements in law and order had played an important role in Bihar's economic recovery after 2005, when the state government under Nitish Kumar placed greater emphasis on policing, criminal prosecution, judicial reforms and administrative accountability.It also highlighted Bihar's significance for India's broader development goals, noting that the state is the country's second most populous and remains its poorest.Bihar's population is estimated at 13.2 crore in 2026, according to the paper, accounting for more than 9 per cent of India's population. It noted that the state's population is larger than that of all but 10 sovereign countries.
Article Summary: Ban failed to reduce crimes against women, says paper by economic think tank NCAER. Prohibition has also hit state revenues, according to the research paper. Education, health and jobs among Bihar's priorities, says the paper. It also highlighted Bihar's significance for India's broader development goals.

Article Title: Pests, mould, live insects: FSSAI suspends license of two food units
Article Text:
Live insects in pistachios, rodent droppings, fungal growth and unhygienic processing among serious violations, FSSAI suspends licences

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has suspended the licences of two food manufacturers in Uttar Pradesh and Maharashtra after inspections uncovered serious food safety violations, including live insects in pistachios, rodent droppings, fungal growth, unhygienic processing conditions and ineffective pest control.The action was taken against VKC Nuts Private Limited (Uttar Pradesh) and Chheda Specialities Foods Pvt Ltd (Maharashtra), with FSSAI saying the deficiencies posed a potential risk to public health.At VKC Nuts, inspectors found live insects in stored pistachios, heavy black mould on storage walls and ceilings, rodent droppings across the premises, rusted machinery, damaged flooring, houseflies on food products and a live lizard near open crates of figs. They also found a food handler sorting figs with a bandaged hand and another handling dry fruits without prescribed corrective spectacles. The unit scored 38% in FSSAI's compliance assessment, following which its licence was partially suspended with immediate effect.At Chheda Specialities Foods, inspectors found workers mixing besan dough with bare hands and peeling bananas on contaminated floors beside decomposing waste.The inspection also found fungal growth around edible oil tanks, wastewater on the processing floor, broken insect-proof mesh, dead houseflies, poor waste management and raw materials stored on wet, dusty floors. Multiple food samples collected during earlier inspections had already been declared unsafe or misbranded, with legal proceedings still underway. The unit recorded a compliance score of 42%.FSSAI said the licences have been suspended in the interest of public health and food safety. Chheda Specialities Foods will remain under suspension until it implements corrective measures and demonstrates full compliance with food safety regulations, while VKC Nuts' partial suspension will continue until further orders.
Article Summary: FSSAI suspends licences of two food manufacturers in Uttar Pradesh and Maharashtra. Inspections uncovered serious food safety violations, including live insects in pistachios, rodent droppings, fungal growth and unhygienic processing conditions. FSSAI said deficiencies posed a potential risk to public health.

NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday addressed IIT Delhi's 57th Convocation Ceremony, urging graduating students to embrace change, keep learning and remember the mentors who shaped their journey.Addressing more than 3,000 graduating students, including 587 PhD scholars, as the chief guest, PM Modi congratulated them on completing their studies and asked them to embrace the next phase of their lives. Article Title: When ‘healthy’ is just a label
Article Text:

“Natural”, “healthy”, “organic”, “heart-friendly”, “high protein” and “zero maida” often persuades a shopper before the packet is even turned over. In a spate of notices sent in the past month, Food Safety and Standards Authority of India ( FSSAI ) has asked several brands whether their front-of-pack promises say more than the product can support.FSSAI has issued notices to food businesses across categories including breads, chocolates, juices, cooking oils, noodles, supplements, packaged water and caffeinated drinks. The claims questioned range from “100% natural” and “organic” to immunity, detoxification, disease reduction and energy-boosting promises. Since these are notices rather than final rulings, the issues remain subject to the companies’ replies and regulatory examination. TOI reached out to FSSAI over e-mail, but was yet to receive a response.The scrutiny comes as India’s health-and-wellness food market expands and brands compete for shoppers seeking healthier choices. Experts say the front of a packet increasingly functions as advertising, while the information needed to judge the product — ingredients, sugar, fat, sodium and additives — is usually on the back.Former FSSAI CEO Pawan Kumar Agarwal says consumers rarely read or fully understand the mandatory information panel.Marketing teams therefore have a powerful incentive to foreground attractive words, sometimes stretching the meaning permitted by regulation. For large companies, he argues, penalties may need to be linked to turnover or the commercial gain from a misleading claim rather than treated as a routine cost.Nutrition experts call this the “health halo” effect: one positive phrase can make the entire product appear healthier and reduce the buyer’s inclination to examine it critically. A packet labelled “natural” can still be high in sugar or sodium. “Sugar-free” does not automatically mean low-carbohydrate. “Organic” requires certification; it is not merely a lifestyle description. Disease-treatment or prevention claims require scientific and regulatory support.AIIMS dietician Monita Gahlot advises shoppers to start with the ingredient list, which records ingredients in descending order by weight. The nutrition panel should then be checked for total and added sugars, saturated and trans fats, sodium, protein and carbohydrates. Serving sizes deserve particular attention: a modest-looking number can be based on a portion far smaller than what people normally consume.The clearest warning sign, food-testing expert Ashwin Bhadri says, is a bold front claim that is not supported or adequately explained elsewhere on the label. The simplest consumer rule is therefore to turn the packet over before deciding.Food author Krish Ashok argues that companies are not acting in a vacuum. Consumers increasingly seek a purchasable shortcut to good health. Products labelled “high protein”, “low GI”, “A2” or “heart-healthy” can offer the feeling of making a healthy choice without the slower work of eating fewer ultra-processed foods, increasing fibre and protein, exercising and sleeping well.That is why tighter enforcement alone will not end the health halo. Brands must make precise, evidence-backed claims, but consumers must also stop treating the front of a packet as nutritional advice.
Article Summary: FSSAI has issued notices to food businesses across categories including breads, chocolates, juices, cooking oils, noodles, supplements, packaged water and caffeinated drinks. The claims questioned range from “100% natural’ and “organic’ to immunity, detoxification, disease reduction and energy-boosting promises.

Article Title: Rijiju vs Rahul over women's quota Bill: Support 'unconditionally' remark gets 'already passed' retort

NEW DELHI: Parliamentary affairs minister Kiren Rijiju on Saturday targeted Lok Sabha leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi over his recent remarks on women’s freedom of expression and challenged him to support the BJP-backed Women’s Reservation Bill “unconditionally”. However, Rahul strongly countered Rijiju's challenge with questioning women Bill's link to delimitation.Rijiju’s remarks came after Rahul Gandhi posted a video calling for greater freedom of expression for women and arguing that India cannot fully develop without women being able to express themselves freely.Responding to the senior Congress leader, Rijiju said Rahul Gandhi’s message appeared to be a positive change and urged the Congress to support the Women’s Reservation Bill without conditions.“This seems to be a positive message from the Congress Party. There's a visible change of heart in Shri Rahul Gandhi Ji about the Women. Now, I hope the Congress Party will support the Women's Reservation Bill unconditionally,” the Union minister posted on X.However, Rahul Gandhi quickly hit back at Rijiju, pointing out that the Women’s Reservation Bill was already passed by Parliament in 2023.The Congress leader then questioned why the Centre is seeking to link the implementation of women’s reservation with the delimitation exercise.Taking to X, Rahul wrote in Hindi, which loosely translates to: "Mr Rijiju, who would know better than you, as the parliamentary affairs minister that the Women's Reservation Bill 2023 has already been passed unanimously, with the full support of the Congress.""The question is, why has it still not been implemented even after three years, and why do you now want to unnecessarily link it to delimitation? Implement the 2023 law. Without any conditions," he added.The Congress and other opposition parties have supported the Women’s Reservation Bill but have opposed linking its implementation to the delimitation exercise. The opposition has demanded that women’s reservation be delinked from delimitation, which would determine the number of Lok Sabha seats.The Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, 2023, was passed by both Houses of Parliament. However, its implementation did not move forward after the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill failed to secure the required two-thirds majority of members present and voting in the Lok Sabha on April 17.The legislation provides for 33% reservation for women in the Lok Sabha and state legislative assemblies and links its implementation to delimitation.Earlier, Rahul said in a social media video that women in India should be given greater freedom to express themselves in all areas of life.He said, “The energy of India's women is trapped. It is not allowed to express itself. It is not allowed to imagine. For me, no country can be successful if its women are not expressing themselves. And I think a lot of my politics, and a lot of what politics should be in this country, is about making people understand that our country is stunted and incomplete without the expression of women.”Rahul further said, “It's not just them doing well in business or politics, but being able to express in their houses, walk the streets comfortably, them putting a point of view that many don't agree with, questioning their parents, husbands, brothers.""A certain amount of freedom from patriarchy and the rigid control men put on women is required if India wants to develop. It has been assaulted and put in the back seat, and we have to bring back women into conversation and allow them to express,” the Congress leader added.The exchange between the two leaders came after Rahul posted his message on women’s freedom following his meeting with Gen Z protesters, where he highlighted the repercussions they have faced amid the crackdown on their protests.

Article Title: QR code, no queue: 25 crore OPD registrations go digital
Article Text:
Long wait at hospital registration counters is slowly giving way to a QR code

NEW DELHI: The long wait at hospital registration counters is slowly giving way to a QR code. In a sign of India's growing digital health footprint, patients have now completed 25 crore outpatient (OPD) registrations through the ABHA-based 'Scan and Register' service under the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM), with nearly four lakh people using the facility every day.Introduced in October 2022, the service allows patients to register for an OPD consultation by simply scanning a QR code displayed at participating hospitals through an ABDM-enabled health app. Once they give consent, their ABHA-linked details are shared with the hospital, eliminating paperwork and reducing waiting time at registration counters.The service is now available in 30,800 hospitals and healthcare facilities across 36 states and Union Territories and 756 districts, making it one of the country's fastest-growing digital public health services. More than 24,000 government facilities and 6,400 private hospitals have adopted the system.The biggest users of the platform are in Bihar, which has recorded over 7.3 crore digital OPD registrations, followed by Uttar Pradesh (4.09 crore), Andhra Pradesh (3.38 crore) and Jammu & Kashmir (1.39 crore).Among hospitals, AIIMS New Delhi has emerged as the country's busiest digital registration centre, recording over 54.29 lakh Scan and Register transactions.It is followed by AIIMS Bhopal (29.1 lakh), AIIMS Bhubaneswar (23.93 lakh), AIIMS Patna (19.62 lakh) and AIIMS Raipur (18.63 lakh).Officials said the service has particularly eased hospital visits for senior citizens, pregnant women and patients requiring frequent follow-ups by cutting time spent at registration counters and doing away with repeated form filling."This milestone reflects the growing trust that citizens and healthcare providers have placed in India's digital health ecosystem. By simplifying one of the most common touchpoints in healthcare, OPD registration, the service has enhanced patient convenience while improving efficiency for hospitals," National Health Authority CEO Dr Sunil Kumar Barnwal said.The National Health Authority said the service is now operational across AIIMS, central and state government hospitals, medical colleges, district hospitals, ESIC and railway hospitals, as well as private healthcare facilities, and is expected to expand further as more hospitals adopt ABHA-enabled digital services.
Article Summary: Patients have now completed 25 crore outpatient (OPD) registrations through the ABHA-based 'Scan and Register' service under the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission. Nearly four lakh people use the facility every day. More than 24,000 government facilities and 6,400 private hospitals have adopted the system.

Article Title: 17.4 lakh blood components discarded in 2025 despite record collection
Article Text:
India discarded over 17.4 lakh blood components in 2025

NEW DELHI: India discarded over 17.4 lakh blood components in 2025, even as blood collection reached a record 1.58 crore units, according to state-wise data tabled in the Rajya Sabha, highlighting continued challenges in blood inventory management despite a steady rise in donations.Available official data indicate that China and India are among the world's largest blood collection programmes. In 2025, India collected 15.71 million units of blood, while China collected 25.5 million units, according to China's National Health Commission.The data, reported by blood centres through the government's e-Raktakosh portal, show that expiry was the leading reason for discarding blood components, followed by reactive units and other operational reasons. Reason-wise discard data has been captured on the portal since 2024, while such details were not available for 2023.Replying to a question in Parliament, the Union health ministry, however, said it had not received any report of regional blood shortages. It added that ensuring an adequate supply of safe blood and minimising wastage is primarily the responsibility of state governments and Union Territories, while the Centre advocates a hub-and-spoke model under which blood is collected and processed at high-volume centres before being distributed to smaller blood banks and storage centres.According to the data, Uttar Pradesh recorded the highest blood collection in 2025 with 21.6 lakh units, followed by Maharashtra (18.73 lakh), Gujarat (11.82 lakh), Rajasthan (10.79 lakh) and Tamil Nadu (9.74 lakh). Overall blood collection increased from 1.42 crore units in 2023 to 1.58 crore units in 2025.The annexure also showed a corresponding increase in blood component utilisation, with Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu and Rajasthan reporting the highest utilisation during 2025.At the same time, Uttar Pradesh reported the highest discard of blood components at 2.40 lakh, followed by Maharashtra (1.87 lakh), Kerala (1.44 lakh), Rajasthan (1.21 lakh) and Tamil Nadu (1.09 lakh). The ministry did not provide an analysis of the wide variation in discard across states.Dr Hema Goyal, Consultant (Blood centre & Lab services), Aakash healthcare said blood wastage is inevitable to some extent, particularly because platelets have a shelf life of only five days. But discarding 17.4 lakh blood components in a year points to a mismatch between collection and actual demand. The solution is not fewer donations but smarter inventory management through real-time stock sharing and better coordination between blood banks.
Article Summary: India discarded over 17.4 lakh blood components in 2025. Blood collection reached a record 1.58 crore units, according to state-wise data tabled in the Rajya Sabha. Expiry was the leading reason for discarding blood, followed by reactive units.

NEW DELHI: In a fresh crackdown on food safety violations, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has acted against two food products, penalising the manufacturer of a fortified sunflower oil after it was found to be substandard and stopping the sale of a Monk Fruit Sweetener over alleged licensing and labelling violations.The regulator imposed a penalty on AWL Agri Business Ltd, Mangaluru, after a laboratory analysis of a retail sample of Fortune "Fryola" Refined Sunflower Seed Oil found that its vitamin D content was below the prescribed standard, making the fortified edible oil substandard under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.FSSAI said the company was given an opportunity to present its case, but the adjudicating authority concluded that it had manufactured and marketed a substandard fortified edible oil before imposing a monetary penalty.In a separate action, the regulator prohibited the sale of PIE Foods' Monk Fruit Sweetener, a natural zero-calorie sugar substitute, after inspections found cartons of the product stored at the company's premises without the required manufacturing licence.FSSAI also alleged that the product carried claims such as "100% Monk Fruit Extract" and "Natural Ingredients", while its online listing did not carry the mandatory endorsement required under food safety regulations.It further said the company failed to produce records showing that the monk fruit extract used in the product had been procured in accordance with the Food Safety and Standards Act.The prohibition order will remain in force until the product complies with the provisions of the Food Safety and Standards Act and related regulations.The regulator said the actions are part of its ongoing drive to tighten enforcement against food business operators and ensure that products sold to consumers meet prescribed safety and quality standards.
Article Summary: The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has acted against two food products. Govt bars firms filing fake drug data from seeking fresh approvals. (Photo: IANS)

In a major crackdown on regulatory fraud in the pharmaceutical sector, the Centre has amended the Drugs Rules, 1945 to empower drug regulators to temporarily debar companies that submit fake or fabricated data while seeking approvals for drugs and related licences.Under the amended rules notified by the Union health ministry on Thursday, applicants found submitting fabricated data will not only face rejection of their applications or cancellation of existing licences, but can also be barred from filing fresh applications before the concerned licensing authority, whether at the Centre or in the states, for a specified period. The action will be taken only after issuing a show-cause notice, and affected applicants will have the right to appeal.The new provision will apply to all applications filed under the Drugs Rules, 1945, and is aimed at deterring companies from submitting false scientific data to secure regulatory approvals.The ministry said regulatory decisions on the quality, safety and efficacy of medicines are based on scientific data submitted by applicants. Fabricated data undermines the integrity of the approval process, raises questions about the quality of medicines and can pose serious risks to public health.The amendment is intended to strengthen accountability and ensure that drug approvals are backed by reliable scientific evidence.Officials said the amendment is part of the government's broader effort to align India's drug regulatory framework with global best practices by promoting ethical compliance while taking stricter action against companies that indulge in malpractice.
Article Summary: New provision will apply to all applications filed under Drugs Rules, 1945. Aim is to deter companies from submitting false scientific data to secure regulatory approvals. Fabricated data undermines the integrity of the approval process, raises questions about the quality of medicines and can pose serious risks to public health.

Article Title: UPI charges: Lok Sabha passes bill for government to make changes
